content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with confidence 0.75. I used the full budget of 60.

**Phase 1.** I trained three tasks that used each rule once: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I compared two test tasks:
- **X = L1-S2-M3:** all three rules already trained, but at most 37.5% overlap in responses with any trained task. It took 32.7 examples on average (6 tests).
- **Y = L1-S4-M1:** one new rule, but 62.5% overlap with a trained task. It took 33 examples on average.

A part-based learner should have found X much easier than Y, since X has no new rules. It didn't, so I ruled part-based out.

**Phase 2.** I trained five more tasks so that X's rules (L1, S2 and M3) each appeared in three trained tasks. None of the new tasks overlapped with X by more than 37.5%, so X's closest match didn't change. I then compared:

| Task | X's rules / C's rules in training | Closest overlap | Mean examples (19 tests each) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X = L1-S2-M3 | each rule in 3 tasks | 37.5% | **17.2** (was 32.7 in phase 1) |
| Control C = L2-S3-M4 | each rule in 1 task | 37.5% | **29.6** |

- **Holistic** predicts X stays the same as before and matches C, because their closest overlap is equal.
- **Part-based** predicts X and C are both cheap, because neither has new rules.
- **Factor-when-justified** predicts what happened: X got cheaper once its rules had appeared enough times to become reusable, and C did not.

The results are noisy (single tests ranged from 1 to 52). The gap between X and C is about 2.8 standard errors, so the evidence is solid but not overwhelming, which is why the confidence is 0.75. I didn't try to work out whether the threshold k is 2 or 3, since the verdict didn't require it.
